32630: His mother, dying in childbirth after hearing that the ark is taken and her husband and father-in-law are dead, names him Ichabod: 'The glory has departed from Israel.'
32631: Ichabod was the son of Phinehas and grandson of Eli, born on the day the ark of God was captured. His name is a lament, meaning roughly 'no glory', because his mother felt God's presence had left Israel. He is mentioned once more as the uncle of a priest who served with Saul.
32632: Born as his mother died; named because 'the glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured' (1 Sam 4:21-22). His brother Ahitub's son Ahijah served as priest under Saul (1 Sam 14:3).
32633: A name more than a speaker; if he spoke, it would be with the weight of a family that lost everything in one day.
32639: When his donkeys stray, Kish sends Saul and a servant to find them. The errand leads Saul to Samuel, who anoints him king.
32640: Kish was a wealthy Benjaminite and the father of Saul, Israel's first king. His lost donkeys set off the chain of events that brought Saul to Samuel. Saul's bones were eventually buried in Kish's family tomb at Zela.
32641: A Benjaminite, 'a man of standing', son of Abiel (1 Sam 9:1). Father of Saul (1 Sam 9:2). Saul and Jonathan buried in his tomb (2 Sam 21:14). Paul names him as Saul's father (Acts 13:21). Genealogies differ on whether Kish's father was Abiel or Ner (1 Chr 8:33), which affects whether Abner was Saul's uncle or cousin.
32642: Practical and well-off; concerned about his animals and then about his missing son.
32646: Higher chronology for David's Hebron reign
32651: After David kills Goliath, Abner brings him, still holding the giant's head, before Saul.
32652: Rebuked by David at the camp
32653: David slips into Saul's camp and takes his spear and water jug, then mocks Abner for failing to guard the king.
32655: After Saul's death he sets up Saul's son Ishbosheth as king over Israel at Mahanaim, opposing David.
32657: His men lose to Joab's at the pool of Gibeon. Fleeing, he kills Joab's brother Asahel, who would not stop chasing him.
32658: Defects to David and is murdered
32659: After quarrelling with Ishbosheth over Saul's concubine Rizpah, he agrees to bring all Israel to David. Joab kills him at Hebron in revenge. David mourns publicly and curses Joab's act.
32660: Abner was Saul's relative and the commander of his army, the most powerful man in Israel after the king. When Saul died he kept the house of Saul alive by making Ishbosheth king, and fought a long war against David. When Ishbosheth accused him over Saul's concubine Rizpah, Abner switched sides and began bringing the northern tribes to David, but Joab murdered him to avenge his brother Asahel. David's public grief, 'a prince and a great man has fallen this day', helped show Israel he had no part in the killing.
32661: Son of Ner, Saul's uncle, and commander of the army (1 Sam 14:50-51). Made Ishbosheth king (2 Sam 2:8-9). Killed Asahel (2 Sam 2:23). Went over to David after the Rizpah quarrel (2 Sam 3:7-21). Killed by Joab at the gate of Hebron (2 Sam 3:27). David wept at his grave (2 Sam 3:31-39).
32662: Many readers see Abner as a realist who served whoever held power, while the narrator uses his death to clear David of blame for the fall of Saul's house.
32663: Loyal to Saul's family for years
32664: Saw that David's rise was God's will (2 Sam 3:9-10)
32666: Used Saul's concubine in a bid for power (2 Sam 3:7)
32667: Ishbosheth's accusation pushes him to David (2 Sam 3:8-12)
32668: Gruff, proud and blunt, a soldier who knows his worth and says so; quick to anger, quick to strike a deal.
32674: king of Israel (northern tribes) after Saul
32676: At forty he is made king over Gilead and the northern tribes and reigns two years, while Judah follows David.
32678: He accuses Abner of sleeping with Saul's concubine Rizpah. Abner explodes and vows to give the kingdom to David; Ishbosheth is too afraid to answer.
32680: At David's demand he takes Michal from her husband Paltiel and sends her back to David.
32682: Two of his captains kill him during his midday rest and bring his head to David, who executes them for murdering an innocent man.
32683: Ish-bosheth was a son of Saul whom Abner made king over the northern tribes after Saul died. He was a weak ruler who depended entirely on Abner. Once Abner defected, his support collapsed, and two of his own officers murdered him in his bed. His original name was probably Eshbaal, 'man of Baal' (where 'baal' may simply mean 'lord'); later scribes seem to have replaced 'baal' with 'bosheth', meaning 'shame'.
32684: Son of Saul, aged forty when he began to reign, reigned two years over Israel (2 Sam 2:8-10). Lost heart when Abner died (2 Sam 4:1). Killed by Rechab and Baanah (2 Sam 4:5-7). Called Eshbaal in Chronicles (1 Chr 8:33).
32686: Most scholars think 'bosheth' (shame) was substituted for 'baal' by scribes who disliked the Baal element; 'baal' may originally have been a title for the LORD (scholarly-consensus on the substitution, debated on the original meaning).
32688: His two-year reign versus David's seven and a half years in Hebron (2 Sam 2:10-11) suggests either a delay before he was crowned or a gap after his death (debated).
32689: Nervous and hesitant; a reluctant king who speaks as if looking over his shoulder for Abner.
32690: From the mouth of shame (likely a scribal change)
32695: He is five when news comes that Saul and Jonathan are dead. His nurse flees with him, he falls, and he is lame in both feet for life.
32697: For Jonathan's sake David restores Saul's land to him and gives him a permanent place at the king's table. He calls himself a 'dead dog' in reply.
32699: During Absalom's revolt his servant Ziba tells David that Mephibosheth stayed in Jerusalem hoping to regain Saul's kingdom. David gives Ziba his property.
32701: Unwashed and unshaven since David left, he says Ziba deceived him. David splits the land between them; Mephibosheth says Ziba may have it all now that the king is safe.
32703: When Saul's descendants are handed to the Gibeonites, David spares him because of his oath to Jonathan.
32704: Mephibosheth was Jonathan's son, lame in both feet after a fall in childhood. David brought him to Jerusalem, restored Saul's lands to him and gave him a seat at the royal table, keeping his covenant of friendship with Jonathan. During Absalom's revolt his servant Ziba accused him of disloyalty, and the text leaves it to the reader to decide who was telling the truth. He became a favourite Christian picture of grace shown to the undeserving.
32705: Lame from age five (2 Sam 4:4). Received Saul's land and ate at David's table 'like one of the king's sons' (2 Sam 9:7-13). Had a young son, Mica (2 Sam 9:12). Accused by Ziba (2 Sam 16:3), defended himself (2 Sam 19:26-28). Spared because of the oath to Jonathan (2 Sam 21:7). Called Merib-baal in Chronicles (1 Chr 8:34). Not the same as Rizpah's son Mephibosheth (2 Sam 21:8).
32706: Often used as an illustration of grace: a crippled enemy's heir welcomed to the king's table for another's sake.
32707: Readers disagree over whether Ziba lied or Mephibosheth was hedging; David's split decision suggests he was not sure either (debated).
32708: Humble to the point of self-abasement, grateful, with a quiet dignity when wronged.
32714: David puts him, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants, in charge of farming Saul's land for Mephibosheth.
32716: He meets the fleeing David with donkeys and food and claims Mephibosheth hopes to regain the throne. David gives Ziba all Mephibosheth's property.
32717: Ziba was a servant of Saul's household whom David made steward of Mephibosheth's estate. During Absalom's revolt he helped David with supplies but accused his master of treachery, winning Mephibosheth's land. When David returned, he split the property between them, unsure whom to believe.
32718: Servant of Saul's house with fifteen sons and twenty servants (2 Sam 9:2-10). Brought provisions and accused Mephibosheth (2 Sam 16:1-4). Mephibosheth said Ziba had slandered him (2 Sam 19:26-27). David divided the land (2 Sam 19:29).
32719: Smooth, eager to please the powerful, always ready with a gift and a story.
32723: Promised to David, given to another
32724: Saul offers her to David if he fights the Philistines, hoping they will kill him, but then gives her to Adriel the Meholathite instead.
32725: Merab was Saul's elder daughter. Saul promised her to David as a reward and a trap, then married her to Adriel instead. Many manuscripts and translations name her as the mother of the five grandsons of Saul later handed over to the Gibeonites, although the traditional Hebrew text there reads 'Michal'.
32726: Saul's elder daughter (1 Sam 14:49). Promised to David, given to Adriel (1 Sam 18:17-19). The five sons whom Michal (or Merab) bore to Adriel were executed by the Gibeonites (2 Sam 21:8-9).
32727: Most modern versions read 'Merab' in 2 Sam 21:8 with some Hebrew and Greek manuscripts, since Adriel was Merab's husband; the KJV keeps 'Michal' and Jewish tradition explains that Michal raised Merab's sons (debated).
32728: Reserved; a royal daughter used as a political piece, speaking little of her own wishes.
32734: Ishbosheth accuses Abner of sleeping with her, which in that culture was a claim to the dead king's throne.
32736: After her two sons and five of Saul's grandsons are executed by the Gibeonites, she spreads sackcloth on a rock and keeps birds and wild animals off the bodies from harvest until the rains. Moved by her vigil, David gives Saul's family an honourable burial.
32737: Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, was a concubine of Saul and mother of his sons Armoni and Mephibosheth (not Jonathan's son). After her sons were executed to end a famine, she kept watch over their bodies for months. Her silent protest moved David to bury Saul and Jonathan's bones properly, and only then 'God responded to the plea for the land'.
32738: Daughter of Aiah, Saul's concubine (2 Sam 3:7). Mother of Armoni and Mephibosheth (2 Sam 21:8). Kept vigil over the bodies (2 Sam 21:10). David then buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam 21:11-14).
32739: Few words; fierce, patient grief that speaks by staying.
32745: Amalekite raiders carry her and Abigail off from Ziklag; David pursues and rescues them.
32747: At Hebron she bears Amnon, David's eldest son.
32748: Ahinoam from Jezreel (a town in Judah, not the northern city) was one of David's earliest wives, married while he was an outlaw. She went with him to Gath and Ziklag and became the mother of Amnon, his firstborn. She should not be confused with Saul's wife Ahinoam, daughter of Ahimaaz, though a few scholars suggest they were the same woman.
32749: David married Ahinoam of Jezreel (1 Sam 25:43). With David at Gath and Ziklag (1 Sam 27:3); taken captive and rescued (1 Sam 30:5). Mother of Amnon (2 Sam 3:2). Saul's wife was also named Ahinoam (1 Sam 14:50).
32750: A minority view (associated with Jon Levenson) proposes that David took Saul's wife Ahinoam, which would explain Nathan's words that God gave David 'your master's wives' (2 Sam 12:8). Most scholars treat them as two different women (speculative).
32751: Quiet and enduring, a woman who shared David's years on the run.
32753: Oppression, or perhaps a place name
32759: She bears Absalom, David's third son, during his reign at Hebron.
32760: Maacah was the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, a small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee, and was probably married to David as part of an alliance. She was the mother of Absalom and almost certainly of Tamar, his full sister. Absalom fled to his grandfather in Geshur after killing Amnon. Several other women in Kings and Chronicles share her name, including Rehoboam's wife and Asa's queen mother.
32761: Daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, mother of Absalom (2 Sam 3:3). Absalom fled to Talmai (2 Sam 13:37-38). Tamar is called Absalom's sister (2 Sam 13:1); that Maacah was her mother is inferred, not stated.
32762: Dignified and foreign-born, a king's daughter in a rival king's court.
32768: He makes himself ill with desire for his half-sister Tamar; his cousin Jonadab suggests he pretend to be sick and ask for her.
32770: When Tamar brings food he seizes her. She pleads with him not to do this 'outrageous thing', but he overpowers her.
32772: His desire turns to hatred and he has her thrown out and the door bolted.
32774: Two years later Absalom invites him to a sheep-shearing feast and has his servants kill him.
32775: Amnon was David's firstborn son and heir. He raped his half-sister Tamar and then cast her out in disgust. David was angry but did nothing, and two years later Tamar's brother Absalom had Amnon murdered. The story is the first fulfilment of Nathan's warning that 'the sword shall never depart' from David's house after his sin with Bathsheba.
32776: Firstborn of David by Ahinoam (2 Sam 3:2). Raped Tamar, then hated her more than he had loved her (2 Sam 13:14-15). David was very angry (2 Sam 13:21) but the Greek text adds that he would not punish Amnon because he loved him as firstborn. Killed by Absalom's men (2 Sam 13:28-29).
32778: The Mishnah (Avot 5:16) contrasts Amnon's love, which depended on something and so ended, with the selfless love of David and Jonathan.
32780: Read as a case study of lust as consumption, of a father's failure to act, and of how sin in David's house repeats his own abuse of power.
32781: Self-pitying, impulsive and entitled; speaks of what he wants, not of the other person.
32786: At David's order she goes to bake bread for her 'sick' half-brother Amnon.
32788: She refuses, calls the act a disgrace in Israel and suggests he ask the king for her properly, but he forces her.
32790: Thrown out, she tears her royal robe, puts ashes on her head and goes away crying. She lives 'desolate' in Absalom's house.
32791: Tamar was David's daughter and Absalom's full sister. Her half-brother Amnon tricked her into his room and raped her, ignoring her clear and courageous protest. She tore her princess's robe and cried aloud rather than stay silent, then lived on in her brother's house as a 'desolate woman'. Absalom named his own daughter after her.
32792: Beautiful sister of Absalom (2 Sam 13:1). Argued against the assault (2 Sam 13:12-13). Tore her long-sleeved robe and mourned (2 Sam 13:18-19). Remained desolate in Absalom's house (2 Sam 13:20). Absalom's daughter was named Tamar (2 Sam 14:27). Listed as David's daughter (1 Chr 3:9).
32794: Tamar is read as a model of a victim's clear voice and as an indictment of a family and court that silenced her ('keep quiet', 2 Sam 13:20).
32796: Often treated mainly as a step in the story of Absalom and as a warning about lust; her own voice received less attention.
32797: Clear, reasoned and brave; she argues from the law and from honour, and then from grief.
32803: As David lies dying, he gathers chariots and runners and holds a feast at En-rogel with Joab and Abiathar, leaving out Nathan, Zadok, Benaiah and Solomon.
32805: Hearing that Solomon has been anointed, his guests scatter. He clings to the horns of the altar until Solomon promises to spare him if he behaves.
32807: Through Bathsheba he asks to marry Abishag, David's last companion. Solomon reads it as a claim to the throne and has Benaiah kill him.
32808: Adonijah, son of David and Haggith, was the eldest surviving son after Amnon and Absalom died, and expected to be king. David had 'never crossed him', and he tried to take the throne while his father was dying, backed by Joab and the priest Abiathar. Nathan and Bathsheba moved David to crown Solomon instead. Adonijah was spared, but after he asked to marry Abishag, Solomon saw a renewed claim to the throne and had him executed.
32809: Son of Haggith, born at Hebron (2 Sam 3:4). Handsome, born after Absalom; David never rebuked him (1 Kgs 1:6). Exalted himself as king (1 Kgs 1:5). Took hold of the altar (1 Kgs 1:50). Admitted the kingdom had become Solomon's 'from the LORD' (1 Kgs 2:15). Killed by Benaiah (1 Kgs 2:25).
32810: Confident and charming, used to getting his way; speaks like the heir he thinks he is.
32814: ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy
32816: Luke traces Jesus' ancestry back through Nathan rather than Solomon.
32817: Nathan was a son of David born in Jerusalem, and one of four sons of Bathsheba (called Bath-shua in Chronicles). He is not the prophet Nathan. His importance is that Luke's genealogy of Jesus runs through him, while Matthew's runs through Solomon.
32818: Born in Jerusalem to David and Bathshua (1 Chr 3:5; 2 Sam 5:14). His house mourns in Zechariah's vision (Zech 12:12). In Jesus' genealogy (Luke 3:31).
32820: Some explain the two genealogies by saying Luke gives Mary's line through Nathan and Matthew gives Joseph's legal line through Solomon (a view going back at least to the Reformation era); others, following Julius Africanus, appeal to levirate marriage (debated).
32821: Many scholars think the two genealogies reflect separate traditions with different theological aims, and that tracing through Nathan avoided the cursed line of Jehoiachin (Jer 22:30) (debated).
32822: Unknown; a quiet royal son remembered mainly for his descendants.
32828: At Bahurim he throws stones and dust at David, calling him a man of blood who stole Saul's throne. David stops Abishai from killing him: 'the LORD has told him' to curse.
32830: When David returns, Shimei hurries to meet him with a thousand Benjaminites and confesses. David swears not to kill him.
32832: On David's deathbed advice, Solomon confines him to Jerusalem. Three years later he goes to Gath after runaway slaves, and Solomon has Benaiah kill him.
32833: Shimei, a relative of Saul, cursed David to his face when David fled from Absalom, blaming him for the fall of Saul's family. David bore it patiently and later pardoned him. But on his deathbed David told Solomon not to let Shimei go unpunished. Solomon restricted him to Jerusalem, and when Shimei broke the terms he was executed.
32834: Of Saul's clan, son of Gera (2 Sam 16:5). Cursed David as a 'man of blood' (2 Sam 16:7-8). Pardoned under oath (2 Sam 19:23). David's charge to Solomon (1 Kgs 2:8-9). Executed after leaving Jerusalem (1 Kgs 2:46).
32836: Some readers admire David's restraint and find his deathbed instruction troubling; others see Solomon's action as lawful because Shimei broke a sworn agreement (debated).
32837: Bitter, loud and partisan; later grovelling and eager to be on the winning side.
32846: He meets David on the Mount of Olives with torn clothes and dust on his head. David sends him back to pretend loyalty to Absalom and defeat Ahithophel's advice.
32848: He greets Absalom with 'Long live the king!' and explains his switch with careful double meanings.
32850: Ahithophel urges an immediate strike on the exhausted David. Hushai paints vivid pictures of David as a bear robbed of her cubs and persuades Absalom to wait and gather all Israel.
32852: He passes the plan to the priests Zadok and Abiathar so David can cross the Jordan in time.
32853: Hushai the Archite held the title 'the king's friend' at David's court. When Absalom rebelled, David sent him back to Jerusalem as a double agent. Hushai won Absalom's trust and talked him out of Ahithophel's sound advice to strike at once, giving David time to escape and regroup. The narrator says this happened because 'the LORD had ordained' to defeat Ahithophel's counsel in answer to David's prayer.
32854: An Archite (2 Sam 15:32), David's friend (2 Sam 15:37; 1 Chr 27:33). Gave advice that seemed better to Absalom, 'for the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel' (2 Sam 17:14). David had prayed that Ahithophel's counsel be turned to foolishness (2 Sam 15:31).
32855: Warm, quick-witted and theatrical; a master of vivid images and loyal double meanings.
32857: Brother of folly (perhaps a deliberate distortion)
32861: Strategic counsel, treated 'as if one consulted the word of God'
32863: Absalom summons him from Giloh. When David hears, he prays that the LORD will turn his counsel to foolishness.
32864: Advises Absalom to take the harem
32865: He tells Absalom to sleep with David's concubines publicly to make the break final; it fulfils Nathan's word (2 Sam 12:11-12).
32867: He proposes to strike David that night with twelve thousand men. When Hushai's plan is preferred, he goes home, puts his affairs in order and hangs himself.
32868: Ahithophel of Giloh was David's most respected adviser, whose counsel was treated almost like an oracle. He joined Absalom's rebellion, perhaps partly from resentment: he seems to have been Bathsheba's grandfather. His plan to strike David immediately would likely have worked, but Absalom followed Hushai instead, and Ahithophel, seeing the revolt was lost, went home and hanged himself.
32869: The Gilonite, David's counsellor (2 Sam 15:12). His advice was esteemed like God's word (2 Sam 16:23). Hanged himself (2 Sam 17:23). His son Eliam was one of David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:34); Bathsheba's father was named Eliam (2 Sam 11:3).
32871: If the two Eliams are the same man, Ahithophel was Bathsheba's grandfather, which would explain his betrayal of David (speculative; the text does not connect them).
32872: Many interpreters see him as a type of Judas: a trusted friend who betrayed the king and then hanged himself (compare Ps 41:9; Matt 27:5).
32873: Cool, precise and coldly practical; speaks in short, confident plans.
32881: He kills two champions of Moab, goes down into a pit on a snowy day and kills a lion, and kills a giant Egyptian with the man's own spear.
32883: David puts him in charge of the foreign royal guard.
32885: With Zadok and Nathan he escorts Solomon on David's mule to be anointed king.
32887: He executes Adonijah, Joab (at the altar) and Shimei, and replaces Joab as army commander.
32888: Benaiah, son of the priest Jehoiada of Kabzeel, was one of David's bravest warriors, famous for killing a lion in a pit on a snowy day. He commanded David's foreign bodyguard and stayed loyal to David's choice of Solomon. Under Solomon he carried out the executions of Adonijah, Joab and Shimei and became commander of the army. His father is a different Jehoiada from the later high priest who protected Joash.
